facts.statement: The species was first described by Edwin Tulley Newton in 1888.
facts.quote: GSM 3166 was described by Edwin Tulley Newton, who loaned it from Rev. Purdon, in 1888.

facts.statement: The genus contains only one species, P. purdoni, which was originally classified as Scaphognathus purdoni before being moved to its own genus in 1919.
facts.quote: It contains a single species, P. purdoni, named initially as a species of the related rhamphorhynchid Scaphognathus in 1888 but moved to its own genus in 1919 on account of a unique combination of characteristics.

facts.statement: While some researchers have referred Parapsicephalus to Dimorphodontia due to its skull shape, it is generally considered a rhamphorhynchid.
facts.quote: This has been the basis of its referral to the Dimorphodontia by some researchers, but it is generally agreed upon that Parapsicephalus probably represents a rhamphorhynchid.

facts.statement: The preserved type skull is 14 cm long, suggesting the animal was of medium size.
facts.quote: The type skull of Parapsicephalus, which is 14 cm long as preserved, suggests that it was of medium size.

facts.statement: Comparisons with related pterosaurs suggest the full skull length was between 18 and 19.6 cm.
facts.quote: Comparisons with the related pterosaurs Scaphognathus, Dorygnathus, and Jianchangnathus indicates that the full skull would have been 18 - 19.6 cm long.

facts.statement: Wingspan estimates range from 1 meter based on early work to 1.68–3.26 meters based on a recently referred 10 cm humerus.
facts.quote: Wellnhofer estimated its wingspan at 1 m; more recently, a referred humerus, which is 10 cm long, has produced wingspan estimates of 1.68 - 3.26 m.

facts.statement: The oval-shaped antorbital fenestra measures 45 mm in length and 24 mm in height.
facts.quote: The oval-shaped antorbital fenestra, situated behind and separate from the nostril, measures 45 mm long and 24 mm tall.

facts.statement: The pear-shaped eye socket measures 34 mm in height and 32 mm in width at its widest point.
facts.quote: The pear-shaped eye socket measures 34 mm tall and 32 mm wide at the widest point.

facts.statement: The exposed part of the brain endocast shows a large flocculus and cerebrum.
facts.quote: which has a large flocculus and cerebrum.

facts.statement: The scapula and coracoid are completely fused, measuring 67 mm and 59 mm respectively, and form a 70° angle creating a V-shaped structure.
facts.quote: The scapula and coracoid appear to be completely fused; they are respectively 67 mm and 59 mm long, and form an angle of 70° to each other, creating overall a V-shaped structure as in Sericipterus.

facts.statement: The describer noted the braincase had intermediate morphology between lizards and birds, suggesting a close relationship between these groups.
facts.quote: In his description of the braincase, he noted its intermediate morphology between that of lizards and birds, which he considered evidence of a close relationship between birds, pterosaurs, and "reptiles".

facts.statement: In 2003, researchers suggested Parapsicephalus was closer to Dorygnathus and formally renamed it Dorygnathus purdoni, though this renaming was not universally adopted.
facts.quote: In 2003, David Unwin, Kenneth Carpenter, and others suggested that Parapsicephalus was actually closer to the roughly contemporaneous Dorygnathus from German deposits. Unwin formally renamed it to the new combination Dorygnathus purdoni.

facts.statement: A specimen of Parapsicephalus was discovered in 2011 at Saltwick Bay.
facts.quote: The specimen NHMUK PV R36634 was found in 2011 within a concretion in Saltwick Bay

facts.statement: A possible additional skull specimen was collected in 1994 from Altdorf, Bavaria, Germany.
facts.quote: An additional possible specimen is a skull collected in 1994 from Altdorf, Bavaria, Germany

facts.statement: The type specimen was collected by Reverend D.W. Purdon in the 1880s.

facts.statement: Parapsicephalus was recognized as a distinct genus in 1919 by Gustav von Arthaber.
facts.quote: Fue reconocido como un género distinto sólo varios años después, en 1919 por Gustav von Arthaber

facts.statement: Parapsicephalus, meaning "behind the head arch," is a rhamphorhynchid pterosaur from the early Toarcian (Early Jurassic) found in the Whitby Alum Shale, Yorkshire, England.
facts.quote: Parapsicephalus (nombre que significa "detrás del arco de la cabeza") fue un género de pterosaurio ranforrincoide de principios del Toarciano (Jurásico Inferior) hallado en el Esquisto Alum de Whitby, Yorkshire, Inglaterra.

facts.statement: Parapsicephalus lived during the Toarcian stage, between 184.2 and 182.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Toarcian to Toarcian (184.2 to 182.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: The known material of Parapsicephalus consists of a partial skull lacking the snout but including a detailed brain cast.
facts.quote: Es conocido de un cráneo parcial que carece del hocico, pero incluye un detallado molde del cerebro.

facts.statement: The prevailing view is that Parapsicephalus is a type of rhamphorhynchid pterosaur.
facts.quote: The prevailing view since Arthaber's renaming of Parapsicephalus as a distinct genus has been that Parapsicephalus represents some kind of rhamphorhynchid

facts.statement: A 2017 analysis found little support for placing Parapsicephalus within the Dimorphodontia.
facts.quote: A 2017 analysis of Parapsicephalus found little support for it being placed in the Dimorphodontia

facts.statement: Affinities with the Rhamphorhynchidae were considered more probable than with Dimorphodontia.
facts.quote: Thus, affinities with the Rhamphorhynchidae were considered more probable.

facts.statement: Parapsicephalus is classified within the family Rhamphorhynchidae.

facts.statement: The Alum Shale Member, where Parapsicephalus fossils are found, was likely deposited in an oxygen-poor, shallow-water environment.
facts.quote: The Alum Shale Member of the Whitby Mudstone Formation was probably deposited in an oxygen-poor, shallow-water environment.

facts.statement: Parapsicephalus lived alongside various marine reptiles including ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs, and thalattosuchians in the Alum Shale locality.
facts.quote: A number of marine reptiles are known from this locality: the ichthyosaurs Stenopterygius, Temnodontosaurus, and Eurhinosaurus; the plesiosaurs Eretmosaurus, Sthenarosaurus, and Microcleidus; and the thalattosuchians Steneosaurus and Pelagosaurus.
